title: SpaceX Just Became a $1.77 Trillion Company. India Won't Let It Turn On Starlink.
excerpt: The biggest IPO in history priced at $135 a share on Thursday. India froze Starlink's final clearance days before the debut.
body:
# SpaceX Just Became a $1.77 Trillion Company. India Won't Let It Turn On Starlink.

Elon Musk's SpaceX priced its initial public offering at $135 per share on Thursday night, raising a record $75 billion and valuing the rocket, satellite, and AI conglomerate at $1.77 trillion. It is the largest IPO in history, surpassing Saudi Aramco's $25.6 billion debut in 2019.

When shares begin trading on the Nasdaq on Friday under the ticker SPCX, SpaceX will instantly rank as the seventh most valuable company in America — worth more than JPMorgan Chase, Berkshire Hathaway, and Eli Lilly.

https://x.com/LaurenDreyer/status/2064426157261668492

But across the Pacific, in what SpaceX's own prospectus identifies as one of Starlink's most important growth markets, the Indian government has just hit pause.

## India Got Cold Feet at the Worst Possible Time

Days before the IPO, Bloomberg reported that India's security regulators under the Ministry of Home Affairs have suspended the final approvals Starlink needs to begin commercial operations in the country. The reason: SpaceX allowed Starlink terminals to operate inside Iran without legal permission, raising concerns in New Delhi about whether it can actually control a U.S.-based satellite operator during a geopolitical crisis.

SpaceX pushed back. "Starlink remains in active and productive discussions with the Government of India," said Lauren Dreyer, SpaceX's VP of Starlink operations, in a social media post.

But the damage to the IPO narrative is real. Starlink is the financial backbone of SpaceX — it generated $11.4 billion in revenue last year, roughly 61 percent of the company's total sales, and it is the only division that makes money. The launch business ran at a loss. The xAI division, which Musk folded into SpaceX earlier this year, lost an unspecified amount, with projections for future losses raising eyebrows among analysts.

Growth in Starlink subscribers is what justifies the $1.77 trillion price tag. India, with 1.4 billion people and vast rural areas where terrestrial broadband remains a pipe dream, is among the largest untapped markets on the planet. For NRIs, the inability of Starlink to operate in India could mean delays in accessing reliable internet services for family members back home, impacting communication and business opportunities.

## The Numbers Behind the Valuation

SpaceX's financials, disclosed for the first time in its S-1 filing, paint a company that is simultaneously the most important infrastructure builder of the space age and a money-losing conglomerate propped up by one profitable product.

Total revenue in 2025 is projected to be $18.67 billion, up 33 percent year-over-year. Net loss is estimated at $4.94 billion, driven almost entirely by xAI's losses. At a $1.77 trillion valuation, the implied revenue multiple is roughly 95x trailing sales — higher than any mega-cap in history at the time of listing.

Oppenheimer initiated coverage on Thursday with an "Outperform" rating and a $190 price target, calling SpaceX "the East India Company of Space" and projecting revenue growth to $200 billion by 2030. Analysts expect Starlink's subscriber base of 10.3 million to grow rapidly if key markets like India, Brazil, and Indonesia open up.

## Musk Did It His Way

The IPO itself was as unconventional as its founder. SpaceX set aside 30 percent of shares for retail investors — an unusually large allocation that bypasses the traditional institutional roadshow. The price was announced at 3 p.m. EDT, while markets were still open, breaking with the standard practice of pricing after the close.

Musk will retain 82 percent of SpaceX's voting power after the IPO, ensuring that he maintains near-absolute control over the company's direction. He also pushed Nasdaq and FTSE Russell to relax their index inclusion criteria, potentially forcing passive funds to buy billions of dollars of SpaceX stock within weeks of listing.

Four U.S. state comptrollers wrote letters to both index providers on Thursday, warning that the rule changes could force retirement funds to purchase stock "that has not proven its value."

## What It Means for India

India's Starlink freeze is not just a regulatory hiccup — it intersects with the country's broader satellite spectrum policy, which remains stuck in a cabinet limbo. The Department of Telecommunications has completed its pricing framework for satellite broadband spectrum, but the proposal awaits cabinet approval, and the Starlink pause has created a knock-on delay.

For Indian consumers, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas where Jio and Airtel's terrestrial networks remain patchy, the delay means continued waiting. For Indian telecom incumbents, it is a reprieve — one that becomes harder to justify as SpaceX's public-market valuation forces a global conversation about who controls orbital internet access.

For NRI investors, SpaceX represents the most consequential public offering since the iPhone-era Apple listings. Shares begin trading Friday, with analysts expecting an afternoon open due to the deal's complexity. Most expect a 10 to 15 percent first-day pop, though Renaissance Capital's Matt Kennedy warned that anything above 50 percent would signal "pure hype."

Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America Securities, Citigroup, and J.P. Morgan are the joint bookrunners.

**Sources**: Reuters, TechCrunch, Investopedia, The Motley Fool, Barron's
